{{distinguish|{{ill|Yokoana-shiki sekishitsu|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber}}}} {{afc comment|1=Contrast with {{ill|Yokoana-shiki sekishitsu|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber}} on enwiki I accidentally conflated Cave tombs and {{ill|Yokoana-shiki sekishitsu|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber}}s a lot but these are distinct[[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 03:15, 27 February 2025 (UTC)}} {{afc comment|1=The category [[:Category:Corridor-type kofun]] was one that I made on enwiki with the erroneous association with {{ill|Yokoana-shiki sekishitsu|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber}}s. If this is ever approved as an enwiki article, immediately run a speedy renaming on that category. Likewise check all links already on enwiki because they are ambiguous between the two articles, apparently even in terms of having both kanji in them, idk how I did something so dumb back then[[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 01:42, 15 March 2025 (UTC)}} [[File:Yoshimi Yoshimi-hyakuana 2.JPG|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Yoshimi Hundred Caves|ja|吉見百穴}} (November 2010)]] [[File:柏谷横穴群.JPG|right|250px|thumb|{{ill|Kashiya Cave Tombs|ja|柏谷横穴群}} (February 2013)]]
'''Cave Tombs''' (横穴墓, Yokōbo/Ouketsubo<ref name="rekihaku">{{Cite web|language=ja|url=https://www.rekihaku.city.yokohama.jp/maibun/qa/detail.php?seq=22|title=Q：横穴墓ってなんて読むのですか?|publisher=Yokohama City Foundation for History and Culture|accessdate=2018-07-28}}</ref>) are burial tombs generally carved into slopes or cliffs, typically measuring around 2 meters in height and extending several meters in depth. These tombs served as burial chambers in ancient East Asia and are most commonly associated with the [[Kofun period]] in Japan, where this burial type emerged and became widely used.
== Characteristics == [[File:市ヶ尾横穴墓群B群.JPG|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Ichigao Cave Tomb Cluster|ja|市ヶ尾横穴墓群}} B Cluster: Forecourt and entrance.]] [[File:出山横穴墓群 2009.03.21 - panoramio (5).jpg|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Deyama Graves|ja|出山横穴墓群|ja|出山横穴墓群}}: Interior view of the burial chamber.]] [[File:楊谷寺谷戸横穴墓群11号墓.jpg|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Yōkokuji Valley Cave Tomb Cluster|ja|楊谷寺谷戸横穴墓群}} Tomb 11: House-shaped chamber.]] [[File:長柄横穴群11号墓棺座.JPG|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Nagara Cave Tomb Cluster|ja|長柄横穴群|1=Nagara Cave Tomb Cluster}} Tomb 11: Stone coffin base.]] Yokohama tombs closely resemble [[kofun]] tombs with horizontal stone chambers. They were carved into rock faces, featuring entrances leading to passageways (羨道, sendō), which open into burial chambers (玄室, genshitsu). These tombs typically lack Kofuns but include exceptions. Burial chambers often feature bases for coffins (棺座, kanza) and showcase various ceiling styles, such as house-shaped, dome-shaped, or arch-shaped. Some tombs incorporate forecourts and intermediate rooms between the passageway and chamber.<ref name="#1">{{Cite book|language=ja|author=Keiji Nagahara|editor=Eiichi Ishigami|title=Iwanami Japanese History Dictionary|publisher=Iwanami Shoten|year=1999|isbn=4-00-080093-0}}</ref>
In {{ill|Kamakura|ja|鎌倉市}}, Yokohama tombs feature the distinctive "Kamakura-type" (鎌倉型横穴墓), where burial shelves or smaller inner chambers were carved into the rear walls of burial chambers.<ref name="#2">{{Cite book|language=ja|author=Sakae Ward Historical Committee|title=The History of Sakae|publisher=Sakae Ward Community Promotion Division|year=2013}}</ref>
Yokohama tombs are typically found in clusters (横穴墓群, yokohama bokun). The {{ill|Yoshimi Hundred Caves|ja|吉見百穴}} in {{ill|Yoshimi|ja|吉見町}}, {{ill|Saitama Prefecture|ja|埼玉県}}, comprises over 200 tombs and is a prominent example designated as a National Historic Site.
Some tombs also feature wall carvings and paintings, often categorized as decorative kofun. Colored embellishments have been discovered in regions such as [[Kyushu]], [[Kanto]], and parts of [[Tohoku]].
== Origins and Evolution == Yokohama tombs originated in northern Kyushu around the late 5th century during the Kofun period and subsequently spread across western Japan, including the San'in, Sanyo, Kinki, and Tokai regions by the mid-6th century. By the early 7th century, they had reached the Hokuriku, Kanto, and southern Tohoku regions. The practice peaked around the time of the {{ill|Thin Burial Edict|ja|薄葬令}} before declining in the late 8th century.<ref name="#1"/>
== Name == Yokohama tombs are sometimes called "yokoana kofun" (横穴古墳), but technically the term "kofun" refers to Kofuns, which these tombs lack. They are often grouped under broader definitions of kofun but differ significantly in their construction and purpose.<ref name="rekihaku"/>
The term "yokohama tombs" became common in the 1960s, gaining popularity among researchers in eastern Japan, whereas western Japan researchers traditionally referred to them as "yokoana." The term "yokohama" is preferred for consistency.<ref name="rekihaku"/>
== Distribution and Notable Cave Tomb Tombs == These tombs are found from Kyushu through San'in, Kinki, Hokuriku, and Tokai, with a high concentration in [[Southern Kantō]]. {{distinguish|{{ill|Yokoana-shiki sekishitsu|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber}}}} {{afc comment|1=Contrast with {{ill|Yokoana-shiki sekishitsu|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber}} on enwiki I accidentally conflated Cave tombs and {{ill|Yokoana-shiki sekishitsu|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber}}s a lot but these are distinct[[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 03:15, 27 February 2025 (UTC)}} {{afc comment|1=The category [[:Category:Corridor-type kofun]] was one that I made on enwiki with the erroneous association with {{ill|Yokoana-shiki sekishitsu|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber}}s. If this is ever approved as an enwiki article, immediately run a speedy renaming on that category. Likewise check all links already on enwiki because they are ambiguous between the two articles, apparently even in terms of having both kanji in them, idk how I did something so dumb back then[[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 01:42, 15 March 2025 (UTC)}} [[File:Yoshimi Yoshimi-hyakuana 2.JPG|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Yoshimi Hundred Caves|ja|吉見百穴}} (November 2010)]] [[File:柏谷横穴群.JPG|right|250px|thumb|{{ill|Kashiya Cave Tombs|ja|柏谷横穴群}} (February 2013)]]
'''Cave Tombs''' (横穴墓, Yokōbo/Ouketsubo<ref name="rekihaku">{{Cite web|language=ja|url=https://www.rekihaku.city.yokohama.jp/maibun/qa/detail.php?seq=22|title=Q：横穴墓ってなんて読むのですか?|publisher=Yokohama City Foundation for History and Culture|accessdate=2018-07-28}}</ref>) are burial tombs generally carved into slopes or cliffs, typically measuring around 2 meters in height and extending several meters in depth. These tombs served as burial chambers in ancient East Asia and are most commonly associated with the [[Kofun period]] in Japan, where this burial type emerged and became widely used.
== Characteristics == [[File:市ヶ尾横穴墓群B群.JPG|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Ichigao Cave Tomb Cluster|ja|市ヶ尾横穴墓群}} B Cluster: Forecourt and entrance.]] [[File:出山横穴墓群 2009.03.21 - panoramio (5).jpg|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Deyama Graves|ja|出山横穴墓群|ja|出山横穴墓群}}: Interior view of the burial chamber.]] [[File:楊谷寺谷戸横穴墓群11号墓.jpg|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Yōkokuji Valley Cave Tomb Cluster|ja|楊谷寺谷戸横穴墓群}} Tomb 11: House-shaped chamber.]] [[File:長柄横穴群11号墓棺座.JPG|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Nagara Cave Tomb Cluster|ja|長柄横穴群|1=Nagara Cave Tomb Cluster}} Tomb 11: Stone coffin base.]] Yokohama tombs closely resemble [[kofun]] tombs with horizontal stone chambers. They were carved into rock faces, featuring entrances leading to passageways (羨道, sendō), which open into burial chambers (玄室, genshitsu). These tombs typically lack Kofuns but include exceptions. Burial chambers often feature bases for coffins (棺座, kanza) and showcase various ceiling styles, such as house-shaped, dome-shaped, or arch-shaped. Some tombs incorporate forecourts and intermediate rooms between the passageway and chamber.<ref name="#1">{{Cite book|language=ja|author=Keiji Nagahara|editor=Eiichi Ishigami|title=Iwanami Japanese History Dictionary|publisher=Iwanami Shoten|year=1999|isbn=4-00-080093-0}}</ref>
In {{ill|Kamakura|ja|鎌倉市}}, Yokohama tombs feature the distinctive "Kamakura-type" (鎌倉型横穴墓), where burial shelves or smaller inner chambers were carved into the rear walls of burial chambers.<ref name="#2">{{Cite book|language=ja|author=Sakae Ward Historical Committee|title=The History of Sakae|publisher=Sakae Ward Community Promotion Division|year=2013}}</ref>
Yokohama tombs are typically found in clusters (横穴墓群, yokohama bokun). The {{ill|Yoshimi Hundred Caves|ja|吉見百穴}} in {{ill|Yoshimi|ja|吉見町}}, {{ill|Saitama Prefecture|ja|埼玉県}}, comprises over 200 tombs and is a prominent example designated as a National Historic Site.
Some tombs also feature wall carvings and paintings, often categorized as decorative kofun. Colored embellishments have been discovered in regions such as [[Kyushu]], [[Kanto]], and parts of [[Tohoku]].
== Origins and Evolution == Yokohama tombs originated in northern Kyushu around the late 5th century during the Kofun period and subsequently spread across western Japan, including the San'in, Sanyo, Kinki, and Tokai regions by the mid-6th century. By the early 7th century, they had reached the Hokuriku, Kanto, and southern Tohoku regions. The practice peaked around the time of the {{ill|Thin Burial Edict|ja|薄葬令}} before declining in the late 8th century.<ref name="#1"/>
== Name == Yokohama tombs are sometimes called "yokoana kofun" (横穴古墳), but technically the term "kofun" refers to Kofuns, which these tombs lack. They are often grouped under broader definitions of kofun but differ significantly in their construction and purpose.<ref name="rekihaku"/>
The term "yokohama tombs" became common in the 1960s, gaining popularity among researchers in eastern Japan, whereas western Japan researchers traditionally referred to them as "yokoana." The term "yokohama" is preferred for consistency.<ref name="rekihaku"/>
== Distribution and Notable Cave Tomb Tombs == These tombs are found from Kyushu through San'in, Kinki, Hokuriku, and Tokai, with a high concentration in [[Southern Kantō]]. The northern limit is thought to be in northern [[Miyagi Prefecture]]. Approximately 3,000 examples exist in [[Shizuoka Prefecture]].

== Origins and Evolution == Yokohama tombs originated in northern Kyushu around the late 5th century during the Kofun period and subsequently spread across western Japan, including the San'in, Sanyo, Kinki, and Tokai regions by the mid-6th century. By the early 7th century, they had reached the Hokuriku, Kanto, and southern Tohoku regions. The practice peaked around the time of the {{ill|Thin Burial Edict|ja|薄葬令}} before declining in the late 8th century.<ref name="#1"/>
== Name == Yokohama tombs are sometimes called "yokoana kofun" (横穴古墳), but technically the term "kofun" refers to Kofuns, which these tombs lack. They are often grouped under broader definitions of kofun but differ significantly in their construction and purpose.<ref name="rekihaku"/>
The term "yokohama tombs" became common in the 1960s, gaining popularity among researchers in eastern Japan, whereas western Japan researchers traditionally referred to them as "yokoana." The term "yokohama" is preferred for consistency.<ref name="rekihaku"/>
== Distribution and Notable Cave Tomb Tombs == These tombs are found from Kyushu through San'in, Kinki, Hokuriku, and Tokai, with a high concentration in [[Southern Kantō]]. The northern limit is thought to be in northern [[Miyagi Prefecture]]. Approximately 3,000 examples exist in [[Shizuoka Prefecture]].

'''Cave Tombs''' (横穴墓, Yokōbo/Ouketsubo<ref name="rekihaku">{{Cite web|language=ja|url=https://www.rekihaku.city.yokohama.jp/maibun/qa/detail.php?seq=22|title=Q：横穴墓ってなんて読むのですか?|publisher=Yokohama City Foundation for History and Culture|accessdate=2018-07-28}}</ref>) are burial tombs generally carved into slopes or cliffs, typically measuring around 2 meters in height and extending several meters in depth. These tombs served as burial chambers in ancient East Asia and are most commonly associated with the [[Kofun period]] in Japan, where this burial type emerged and became widely used.
== Characteristics == [[File:市ヶ尾横穴墓群B群.JPG|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Ichigao Cave Tomb Cluster|ja|市ヶ尾横穴墓群}} B Cluster: Forecourt and entrance.]] [[File:出山横穴墓群 2009.03.21 - panoramio (5).jpg|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Deyama Graves|ja|出山横穴墓群|ja|出山横穴墓群}}: Interior view of the burial chamber.]] [[File:楊谷寺谷戸横穴墓群11号墓.jpg|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Yōkokuji Valley Cave Tomb Cluster|ja|楊谷寺谷戸横穴墓群}} Tomb 11: House-shaped chamber.]] [[File:長柄横穴群11号墓棺座.JPG|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Nagara Cave Tomb Cluster|ja|長柄横穴群|1=Nagara Cave Tomb Cluster}} Tomb 11: Stone coffin base.]] Yokohama tombs closely resemble [[kofun]] tombs with horizontal stone chambers. They were carved into rock faces, featuring entrances leading to passageways (羨道, sendō), which open into burial chambers (玄室, genshitsu). These tombs typically lack Kofuns but include exceptions. Burial chambers often feature bases for coffins (棺座, kanza) and showcase various ceiling styles, such as house-shaped, dome-shaped, or arch-shaped. Some tombs incorporate forecourts and intermediate rooms between the passageway and chamber.<ref name="#1">{{Cite book|language=ja|author=Keiji Nagahara|editor=Eiichi Ishigami|title=Iwanami Japanese History Dictionary|publisher=Iwanami Shoten|year=1999|isbn=4-00-080093-0}}</ref>
In {{ill|Kamakura|ja|鎌倉市}}, Yokohama tombs feature the distinctive "Kamakura-type" (鎌倉型横穴墓), where burial shelves or smaller inner chambers were carved into the rear walls of burial chambers.<ref name="#2">{{Cite book|language=ja|author=Sakae Ward Historical Committee|title=The History of Sakae|publisher=Sakae Ward Community Promotion Division|year=2013}}</ref>
Yokohama tombs are typically found in clusters (横穴墓群, yokohama bokun). The {{ill|Yoshimi Hundred Caves|ja|吉見百穴}} in {{ill|Yoshimi|ja|吉見町}}, {{ill|Saitama Prefecture|ja|埼玉県}}, comprises over 200 tombs and is a prominent example designated as a National Historic Site.

By the early 7th century, they had reached the Hokuriku, Kanto, and southern Tohoku regions. The practice peaked around the time of the {{ill|Thin Burial Edict|ja|薄葬令}} before declining in the late 8th century.<ref name="#1"/>

{{distinguish|{{ill|Yokoana-shiki sekishitsu|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber}}}} {{afc comment|1=Contrast with {{ill|Yokoana-shiki sekishitsu|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber}} on enwiki I accidentally conflated Cave tombs and {{ill|Yokoana-shiki sekishitsu|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber}}s a lot but these are distinct[[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 03:15, 27 February 2025 (UTC)}} {{afc comment|1=The category [[:Category:Corridor-type kofun]] was one that I made on enwiki with the erroneous association with {{ill|Yokoana-shiki sekishitsu|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber}}s. If this is ever approved as an enwiki article, immediately run a speedy renaming on that category. Likewise check all links already on enwiki because they are ambiguous between the two articles, apparently even in terms of having both kanji in them, idk how I did something so dumb back then[[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 01:42, 15 March 2025 (UTC)}} [[File:Yoshimi Yoshimi-hyakuana 2.JPG|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Yoshimi Hundred Caves|ja|吉見百穴}} (November 2010)]] [[File:柏谷横穴群.JPG|right|250px|thumb|{{ill|Kashiya Cave Tombs|ja|柏谷横穴群}} (February 2013)]]
'''Cave Tombs''' (横穴墓, Yokōbo/Ouketsubo<ref name="rekihaku">{{Cite web|language=ja|url=https://www.rekihaku.city.yokohama.jp/maibun/qa/detail.php?seq=22|title=Q：横穴墓ってなんて読むのですか?|publisher=Yokohama City Foundation for History and Culture|accessdate=2018-07-28}}</ref>) are burial tombs generally carved into slopes or cliffs, typically measuring around 2 meters in height and extending several meters in depth. These tombs served as burial chambers in ancient East Asia and are most commonly associated with the [[Kofun period]] in Japan, where this burial type emerged and became widely used.
== Characteristics == [[File:市ヶ尾横穴墓群B群.JPG|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Ichigao Cave Tomb Cluster|ja|市ヶ尾横穴墓群}} B Cluster: Forecourt and entrance.]] [[File:出山横穴墓群 2009.03.21 - panoramio (5).jpg|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Deyama Graves|ja|出山横穴墓群|ja|出山横穴墓群}}: Interior view of the burial chamber.]] [[File:楊谷寺谷戸横穴墓群11号墓.jpg|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Yōkokuji Valley Cave Tomb Cluster|ja|楊谷寺谷戸横穴墓群}} Tomb 11: House-shaped chamber.]] [[File:長柄横穴群11号墓棺座.JPG|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Nagara Cave Tomb Cluster|ja|長柄横穴群|1=Nagara Cave Tomb Cluster}} Tomb 11: Stone coffin base.]] Yokohama tombs closely resemble [[kofun]] tombs with horizontal stone chambers. They were carved into rock faces, featuring entrances leading to passageways (羨道, sendō), which open into burial chambers (玄室, genshitsu). These tombs typically lack Kofuns but include exceptions. Burial chambers often feature bases for coffins (棺座, kanza) and showcase various ceiling styles, such as house-shaped, dome-shaped, or arch-shaped. Some tombs incorporate forecourts and intermediate rooms between the passageway and chamber.<ref name="#1">{{Cite book|language=ja|author=Keiji Nagahara|editor=Eiichi Ishigami|title=Iwanami Japanese History Dictionary|publisher=Iwanami Shoten|year=1999|isbn=4-00-080093-0}}</ref>
In {{ill|Kamakura|ja|鎌倉市}}, Yokohama tombs feature the distinctive "Kamakura-type" (鎌倉型横穴墓), where burial shelves or smaller inner chambers were carved into the rear walls of burial chambers.<ref name="#2">{{Cite book|language=ja|author=Sakae Ward Historical Committee|title=The History of Sakae|publisher=Sakae Ward Community Promotion Division|year=2013}}</ref>
Yokohama tombs are typically found in clusters (横穴墓群, yokohama bokun). The {{ill|Yoshimi Hundred Caves|ja|吉見百穴}} in {{ill|Yoshimi|ja|吉見町}}, {{ill|Saitama Prefecture|ja|埼玉県}}, comprises over 200 tombs and is a prominent example designated as a National Historic Site.
Some tombs also feature wall carvings and paintings, often categorized as decorative kofun. Colored embellishments have been discovered in regions such as [[Kyushu]], [[Kanto]], and parts of [[Tohoku]].
== Origins and Evolution == Yokohama tombs originated in northern Kyushu around the late 5th century during the Kofun period and subsequently spread across western Japan, including the San'in, Sanyo, Kinki, and Tokai regions by the mid-6th century. By the early 7th century, they had reached the Hokuriku, Kanto, and southern Tohoku regions. The practice peaked around the time of the {{ill|Thin Burial Edict|ja|薄葬令}} before declining in the late 8th century.<ref name="#1"/>
== Name == Yokohama tombs are sometimes called "yokoana kofun" (横穴古墳), but technically the term "kofun" refers to Kofuns, which these tombs lack. They are often grouped under broader definitions of kofun but differ significantly in their construction and purpose.<ref name="rekihaku"/>
The term "yokohama tombs" became common in the 1960s, gaining popularity among researchers in eastern Japan, whereas western Japan researchers traditionally referred to them as "yokoana." The term "yokohama" is preferred for consistency.<ref name="rekihaku"/>
== Distribution and Notable Cave Tomb Tombs == These tombs are found from Kyushu through San'in, Kinki, Hokuriku, and Tokai, with a high concentration in [[Southern Kantō]]. The northern limit is thought to be in northern [[Miyagi Prefecture]]. Approximately 3,000 examples exist in [[Shizuoka Prefecture]].

14 tombs * {{ill|Todoroki Ravine Cave Tomb Cluster|ja|谷沢川横穴群}} ({{ill|Setagaya|ja|世田谷区}}, Tokyo) * {{ill|Ekoda Cave Tomb Cluster|ja|荏子田横穴}} ({{ill|Aoba-ku, Yokohama|ja|青葉区}}, {{ill|Yokohama|ja|横浜市}}, [[Kanagawa Prefecture]]) - Municipal Historic Site, 2 tombs * {{ill|Ichigao Cave Tomb Cluster|ja|市ヶ尾横穴古墳群|1=Ichigao Cave Tomb Cluster}} (Aoba-ku, Yokohama) - Prefectural Historic Site, 19 tombs * {{ill|Itachigawa Basin Rock-Cut Tombs|ja|㹨川流域横穴墓群|ja|㹨川流域横穴墓群}} (Kamakura-style tomb concentration) ** {{ill|Matsugasaki Cave Tomb Cluster|ja|松ヶ崎横穴墓群}} ({{ill|Kōnan-ku, Yokohama|ja|港南区}}, Yokohama) - Municipal Historic Site, 8 tombs ** {{ill|Shichisekiyama Cave Tomb Cluster|ja|七石山横穴墓群|ja|七石山横穴墓群}} ({{ill|Sakae-ku, Yokohama|ja|栄区}}, Yokohama) - Over 100 tombs originally ** {{ill|Miyanomae Tunnel Tomb Cluster|ja|宮ノ前横穴墓群}} (Sakae-ku, Yokohama) - 23 tombs ** {{ill|Hikoshigaya Cave Tomb Cluster|ja|ひこしヶ谷横穴墓群}} (Sakae-ku, Yokohama) - 12 tombs
=== Tokai Region === * {{ill|Kashiya Cave Tombs|ja|柏谷横穴群|ja|柏谷横穴群}} ({{ill|Kannami|ja|函南町}}, [[Shizuoka Prefecture]]) - National Historic Site, 106 tombs * {{ill|Kitaema Cave Tomb Cluster|ja|北江間横穴群}} ({{ill|Izunokuni|ja|伊豆の国市}}, Shizuoka) - National Historic Site, 101 tombs * {{ill|E-no-ura Cave Tomb Cluster|ja|江浦横穴群}} ({{ill|Numazu|ja|沼津市}}, Shizuoka) - Prefectural Historic Site, 92 tombs

== Origins and Evolution == Yokohama tombs originated in northern Kyushu around the late 5th century during the Kofun period and subsequently spread across western Japan, including the San'in, Sanyo, Kinki, and Tokai regions by the mid-6th century. By the early 7th century, they had reached the Hokuriku, Kanto, and southern Tohoku regions. The practice peaked around the time of the {{ill|Thin Burial Edict|ja|薄葬令}} before declining in the late 8th century.<ref name="#1"/>
== Name == Yokohama tombs are sometimes called "yokoana kofun" (横穴古墳), but technically the term "kofun" refers to Kofuns, which these tombs lack. They are often grouped under broader definitions of kofun but differ significantly in their construction and purpose.<ref name="rekihaku"/>
The term "yokohama tombs" became common in the 1960s, gaining popularity among researchers in eastern Japan, whereas western Japan researchers traditionally referred to them as "yokoana." The term "yokohama" is preferred for consistency.<ref name="rekihaku"/>
== Distribution and Notable Cave Tomb Tombs == These tombs are found from Kyushu through San'in, Kinki, Hokuriku, and Tokai, with a high concentration in [[Southern Kantō]]. The northern limit is thought to be in northern [[Miyagi Prefecture]]. Approximately 3,000 examples exist in [[Shizuoka Prefecture]].

'''Cave Tombs''' (横穴墓, Yokōbo/Ouketsubo<ref name="rekihaku">{{Cite web|language=ja|url=https://www.rekihaku.city.yokohama.jp/maibun/qa/detail.php?seq=22|title=Q：横穴墓ってなんて読むのですか?|publisher=Yokohama City Foundation for History and Culture|accessdate=2018-07-28}}</ref>) are burial tombs generally carved into slopes or cliffs, typically measuring around 2 meters in height and extending several meters in depth. These tombs served as burial chambers in ancient East Asia and are most commonly associated with the [[Kofun period]] in Japan, where this burial type emerged and became widely used.
== Characteristics == [[File:市ヶ尾横穴墓群B群.JPG|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Ichigao Cave Tomb Cluster|ja|市ヶ尾横穴墓群}} B Cluster: Forecourt and entrance.]] [[File:出山横穴墓群 2009.03.21 - panoramio (5).jpg|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Deyama Graves|ja|出山横穴墓群|ja|出山横穴墓群}}: Interior view of the burial chamber.]] [[File:楊谷寺谷戸横穴墓群11号墓.jpg|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Yōkokuji Valley Cave Tomb Cluster|ja|楊谷寺谷戸横穴墓群}} Tomb 11: House-shaped chamber.]] [[File:長柄横穴群11号墓棺座.JPG|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Nagara Cave Tomb Cluster|ja|長柄横穴群|1=Nagara Cave Tomb Cluster}} Tomb 11: Stone coffin base.]] Yokohama tombs closely resemble [[kofun]] tombs with horizontal stone chambers. They were carved into rock faces, featuring entrances leading to passageways (羨道, sendō), which open into burial chambers (玄室, genshitsu). These tombs typically lack Kofuns but include exceptions. Burial chambers often feature bases for coffins (棺座, kanza) and showcase various ceiling styles, such as house-shaped, dome-shaped, or arch-shaped. Some tombs incorporate forecourts and intermediate rooms between the passageway and chamber.<ref name="#1">{{Cite book|language=ja|author=Keiji Nagahara|editor=Eiichi Ishigami|title=Iwanami Japanese History Dictionary|publisher=Iwanami Shoten|year=1999|isbn=4-00-080093-0}}</ref>
In {{ill|Kamakura|ja|鎌倉市}}, Yokohama tombs feature the distinctive "Kamakura-type" (鎌倉型横穴墓), where burial shelves or smaller inner chambers were carved into the rear walls of burial chambers.<ref name="#2">{{Cite book|language=ja|author=Sakae Ward Historical Committee|title=The History of Sakae|publisher=Sakae Ward Community Promotion Division|year=2013}}</ref>
Yokohama tombs are typically found in clusters (横穴墓群, yokohama bokun). The {{ill|Yoshimi Hundred Caves|ja|吉見百穴}} in {{ill|Yoshimi|ja|吉見町}}, {{ill|Saitama Prefecture|ja|埼玉県}}, comprises over 200 tombs and is a prominent example designated as a National Historic Site.

By the early 7th century, they had reached the Hokuriku, Kanto, and southern Tohoku regions. The practice peaked around the time of the {{ill|Thin Burial Edict|ja|薄葬令}} before declining in the late 8th century.<ref name="#1"/>

{{distinguish|{{ill|Yokoana-shiki sekishitsu|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber}}}} {{afc comment|1=Contrast with {{ill|Yokoana-shiki sekishitsu|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber}} on enwiki I accidentally conflated Cave tombs and {{ill|Yokoana-shiki sekishitsu|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber}}s a lot but these are distinct[[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 03:15, 27 February 2025 (UTC)}} {{afc comment|1=The category [[:Category:Corridor-type kofun]] was one that I made on enwiki with the erroneous association with {{ill|Yokoana-shiki sekishitsu|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber}}s. If this is ever approved as an enwiki article, immediately run a speedy renaming on that category. Likewise check all links already on enwiki because they are ambiguous between the two articles, apparently even in terms of having both kanji in them, idk how I did something so dumb back then[[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 01:42, 15 March 2025 (UTC)}} [[File:Yoshimi Yoshimi-hyakuana 2.JPG|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Yoshimi Hundred Caves|ja|吉見百穴}} (November 2010)]] [[File:柏谷横穴群.JPG|right|250px|thumb|{{ill|Kashiya Cave Tombs|ja|柏谷横穴群}} (February 2013)]]
'''Cave Tombs''' (横穴墓, Yokōbo/Ouketsubo<ref name="rekihaku">{{Cite web|language=ja|url=https://www.rekihaku.city.yokohama.jp/maibun/qa/detail.php?seq=22|title=Q：横穴墓ってなんて読むのですか?|publisher=Yokohama City Foundation for History and Culture|accessdate=2018-07-28}}</ref>) are burial tombs generally carved into slopes or cliffs, typically measuring around 2 meters in height and extending several meters in depth. These tombs served as burial chambers in ancient East Asia and are most commonly associated with the [[Kofun period]] in Japan, where this burial type emerged and became widely used.
== Characteristics == [[File:市ヶ尾横穴墓群B群.JPG|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Ichigao Cave Tomb Cluster|ja|市ヶ尾横穴墓群}} B Cluster: Forecourt and entrance.]] [[File:出山横穴墓群 2009.03.21 - panoramio (5).jpg|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Deyama Graves|ja|出山横穴墓群|ja|出山横穴墓群}}: Interior view of the burial chamber.]] [[File:楊谷寺谷戸横穴墓群11号墓.jpg|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Yōkokuji Valley Cave Tomb Cluster|ja|楊谷寺谷戸横穴墓群}} Tomb 11: House-shaped chamber.]] [[File:長柄横穴群11号墓棺座.JPG|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Nagara Cave Tomb Cluster|ja|長柄横穴群|1=Nagara Cave Tomb Cluster}} Tomb 11: Stone coffin base.]] Yokohama tombs closely resemble [[kofun]] tombs with horizontal stone chambers. They were carved into rock faces, featuring entrances leading to passageways (羨道, sendō), which open into burial chambers (玄室, genshitsu). These tombs typically lack Kofuns but include exceptions. Burial chambers often feature bases for coffins (棺座, kanza) and showcase various ceiling styles, such as house-shaped, dome-shaped, or arch-shaped. Some tombs incorporate forecourts and intermediate rooms between the passageway and chamber.<ref name="#1">{{Cite book|language=ja|author=Keiji Nagahara|editor=Eiichi Ishigami|title=Iwanami Japanese History Dictionary|publisher=Iwanami Shoten|year=1999|isbn=4-00-080093-0}}</ref>
In {{ill|Kamakura|ja|鎌倉市}}, Yokohama tombs feature the distinctive "Kamakura-type" (鎌倉型横穴墓), where burial shelves or smaller inner chambers were carved into the rear walls of burial chambers.<ref name="#2">{{Cite book|language=ja|author=Sakae Ward Historical Committee|title=The History of Sakae|publisher=Sakae Ward Community Promotion Division|year=2013}}</ref>
Yokohama tombs are typically found in clusters (横穴墓群, yokohama bokun). The {{ill|Yoshimi Hundred Caves|ja|吉見百穴}} in {{ill|Yoshimi|ja|吉見町}}, {{ill|Saitama Prefecture|ja|埼玉県}}, comprises over 200 tombs and is a prominent example designated as a National Historic Site.
Some tombs also feature wall carvings and paintings, often categorized as decorative kofun. Colored embellishments have been discovered in regions such as [[Kyushu]], [[Kanto]], and parts of [[Tohoku]].
== Origins and Evolution == Yokohama tombs originated in northern Kyushu around the late 5th century during the Kofun period and subsequently spread across western Japan, including the San'in, Sanyo, Kinki, and Tokai regions by the mid-6th century. By the early 7th century, they had reached the Hokuriku, Kanto, and southern Tohoku regions. The practice peaked around the time of the {{ill|Thin Burial Edict|ja|薄葬令}} before declining in the late 8th century.<ref name="#1"/>
== Name == Yokohama tombs are sometimes called "yokoana kofun" (横穴古墳), but technically the term "kofun" refers to Kofuns, which these tombs lack. They are often grouped under broader definitions of kofun but differ significantly in their construction and purpose.<ref name="rekihaku"/>
The term "yokohama tombs" became common in the 1960s, gaining popularity among researchers in eastern Japan, whereas western Japan researchers traditionally referred to them as "yokoana." The term "yokohama" is preferred for consistency.<ref name="rekihaku"/>
== Distribution and Notable Cave Tomb Tombs == These tombs are found from Kyushu through San'in, Kinki, Hokuriku, and Tokai, with a high concentration in [[Southern Kantō]]. The northern limit is thought to be in northern [[Miyagi Prefecture]]. Approximately 3,000 examples exist in [[Shizuoka Prefecture]].

Some tombs also feature wall carvings and paintings, often categorized as decorative kofun. Colored embellishments have been discovered in regions such as [[Kyushu]], [[Kanto]], and parts of [[Tohoku]].
== Origins and Evolution == Yokohama tombs originated in northern Kyushu around the late 5th century during the Kofun period and subsequently spread across western Japan, including the San'in, Sanyo, Kinki, and Tokai regions by the mid-6th century. By the early 7th century, they had reached the Hokuriku, Kanto, and southern Tohoku regions. The practice peaked around the time of the {{ill|Thin Burial Edict|ja|薄葬令}} before declining in the late 8th century.<ref name="#1"/>
== Name == Yokohama tombs are sometimes called "yokoana kofun" (横穴古墳), but technically the term "kofun" refers to Kofuns, which these tombs lack. They are often grouped under broader definitions of kofun but differ significantly in their construction and purpose.<ref name="rekihaku"/>
The term "yokohama tombs" became common in the 1960s, gaining popularity among researchers in eastern Japan, whereas western Japan researchers traditionally referred to them as "yokoana." The term "yokohama" is preferred for consistency.<ref name="rekihaku"/>
== Distribution and Notable Cave Tomb Tombs == These tombs are found from Kyushu through San'in, Kinki, Hokuriku, and Tokai, with a high concentration in [[Southern Kantō]]. The northern limit is thought to be in northern [[Miyagi Prefecture]]. Approximately 3,000 examples exist in [[Shizuoka Prefecture]].

'''Cave Tombs''' (横穴墓, Yokōbo/Ouketsubo<ref name="rekihaku">{{Cite web|language=ja|url=https://www.rekihaku.city.yokohama.jp/maibun/qa/detail.php?seq=22|title=Q：横穴墓ってなんて読むのですか?|publisher=Yokohama City Foundation for History and Culture|accessdate=2018-07-28}}</ref>) are burial tombs generally carved into slopes or cliffs, typically measuring around 2 meters in height and extending several meters in depth. These tombs served as burial chambers in ancient East Asia and are most commonly associated with the [[Kofun period]] in Japan, where this burial type emerged and became widely used.
== Characteristics == [[File:市ヶ尾横穴墓群B群.JPG|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Ichigao Cave Tomb Cluster|ja|市ヶ尾横穴墓群}} B Cluster: Forecourt and entrance.]] [[File:出山横穴墓群 2009.03.21 - panoramio (5).jpg|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Deyama Graves|ja|出山横穴墓群|ja|出山横穴墓群}}: Interior view of the burial chamber.]] [[File:楊谷寺谷戸横穴墓群11号墓.jpg|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Yōkokuji Valley Cave Tomb Cluster|ja|楊谷寺谷戸横穴墓群}} Tomb 11: House-shaped chamber.]] [[File:長柄横穴群11号墓棺座.JPG|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Nagara Cave Tomb Cluster|ja|長柄横穴群|1=Nagara Cave Tomb Cluster}} Tomb 11: Stone coffin base.]] Yokohama tombs closely resemble [[kofun]] tombs with horizontal stone chambers. They were carved into rock faces, featuring entrances leading to passageways (羨道, sendō), which open into burial chambers (玄室, genshitsu). These tombs typically lack Kofuns but include exceptions. Burial chambers often feature bases for coffins (棺座, kanza) and showcase various ceiling styles, such as house-shaped, dome-shaped, or arch-shaped. Some tombs incorporate forecourts and intermediate rooms between the passageway and chamber.<ref name="#1">{{Cite book|language=ja|author=Keiji Nagahara|editor=Eiichi Ishigami|title=Iwanami Japanese History Dictionary|publisher=Iwanami Shoten|year=1999|isbn=4-00-080093-0}}</ref>
In {{ill|Kamakura|ja|鎌倉市}}, Yokohama tombs feature the distinctive "Kamakura-type" (鎌倉型横穴墓), where burial shelves or smaller inner chambers were carved into the rear walls of burial chambers.<ref name="#2">{{Cite book|language=ja|author=Sakae Ward Historical Committee|title=The History of Sakae|publisher=Sakae Ward Community Promotion Division|year=2013}}</ref>
Yokohama tombs are typically found in clusters (横穴墓群, yokohama bokun). The {{ill|Yoshimi Hundred Caves|ja|吉見百穴}} in {{ill|Yoshimi|ja|吉見町}}, {{ill|Saitama Prefecture|ja|埼玉県}}, comprises over 200 tombs and is a prominent example designated as a National Historic Site.

The practice peaked around the time of the {{ill|Thin Burial Edict|ja|薄葬令}} before declining in the late 8th century.<ref name="#1"/>

'''Cave Tombs''' (横穴墓, Yokōbo/Ouketsubo<ref name="rekihaku">{{Cite web|language=ja|url=https://www.rekihaku.city.yokohama.jp/maibun/qa/detail.php?seq=22|title=Q：横穴墓ってなんて読むのですか?|publisher=Yokohama City Foundation for History and Culture|accessdate=2018-07-28}}</ref>) are burial tombs generally carved into slopes or cliffs, typically measuring around 2 meters in height and extending several meters in depth. These tombs served as burial chambers in ancient East Asia and are most commonly associated with the [[Kofun period]] in Japan, where this burial type emerged and became widely used.
== Characteristics == [[File:市ヶ尾横穴墓群B群.JPG|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Ichigao Cave Tomb Cluster|ja|市ヶ尾横穴墓群}} B Cluster: Forecourt and entrance.]] [[File:出山横穴墓群 2009.03.21 - panoramio (5).jpg|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Deyama Graves|ja|出山横穴墓群|ja|出山横穴墓群}}: Interior view of the burial chamber.]] [[File:楊谷寺谷戸横穴墓群11号墓.jpg|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Yōkokuji Valley Cave Tomb Cluster|ja|楊谷寺谷戸横穴墓群}} Tomb 11: House-shaped chamber.]] [[File:長柄横穴群11号墓棺座.JPG|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Nagara Cave Tomb Cluster|ja|長柄横穴群|1=Nagara Cave Tomb Cluster}} Tomb 11: Stone coffin base.]] Yokohama tombs closely resemble [[kofun]] tombs with horizontal stone chambers. They were carved into rock faces, featuring entrances leading to passageways (羨道, sendō), which open into burial chambers (玄室, genshitsu). These tombs typically lack Kofuns but include exceptions. Burial chambers often feature bases for coffins (棺座, kanza) and showcase various ceiling styles, such as house-shaped, dome-shaped, or arch-shaped. Some tombs incorporate forecourts and intermediate rooms between the passageway and chamber.<ref name="#1">{{Cite book|language=ja|author=Keiji Nagahara|editor=Eiichi Ishigami|title=Iwanami Japanese History Dictionary|publisher=Iwanami Shoten|year=1999|isbn=4-00-080093-0}}</ref>
In {{ill|Kamakura|ja|鎌倉市}}, Yokohama tombs feature the distinctive "Kamakura-type" (鎌倉型横穴墓), where burial shelves or smaller inner chambers were carved into the rear walls of burial chambers.<ref name="#2">{{Cite book|language=ja|author=Sakae Ward Historical Committee|title=The History of Sakae|publisher=Sakae Ward Community Promotion Division|year=2013}}</ref>
Yokohama tombs are typically found in clusters (横穴墓群, yokohama bokun). The {{ill|Yoshimi Hundred Caves|ja|吉見百穴}} in {{ill|Yoshimi|ja|吉見町}}, {{ill|Saitama Prefecture|ja|埼玉県}}, comprises over 200 tombs and is a prominent example designated as a National Historic Site.
Some tombs also feature wall carvings and paintings, often categorized as decorative kofun. Colored embellishments have been discovered in regions such as [[Kyushu]], [[Kanto]], and parts of [[Tohoku]].
== Origins and Evolution == Yokohama tombs originated in northern Kyushu around the late 5th century during the Kofun period and subsequently spread across western Japan, including the San'in, Sanyo, Kinki, and Tokai regions by the mid-6th century. By the early 7th century, they had reached the Hokuriku, Kanto, and southern Tohoku regions. The practice peaked around the time of the {{ill|Thin Burial Edict|ja|薄葬令}} before declining in the late 8th century.<ref name="#1"/>
== Name == Yokohama tombs are sometimes called "yokoana kofun" (横穴古墳), but technically the term "kofun" refers to Kofuns, which these tombs lack. They are often grouped under broader definitions of kofun but differ significantly in their construction and purpose.<ref name="rekihaku"/>
The term "yokohama tombs" became common in the 1960s, gaining popularity among researchers in eastern Japan, whereas western Japan researchers traditionally referred to them as "yokoana." The term "yokohama" is preferred for consistency.<ref name="rekihaku"/>
== Distribution and Notable Cave Tomb Tombs == These tombs are found from Kyushu through San'in, Kinki, Hokuriku, and Tokai, with a high concentration in [[Southern Kantō]]. The northern limit is thought to be in northern [[Miyagi Prefecture]]. Approximately 3,000 examples exist in [[Shizuoka Prefecture]].

Burial chambers often feature bases for coffins (棺座, kanza) and showcase various ceiling styles, such as house-shaped, dome-shaped, or arch-shaped. Some tombs incorporate forecourts and intermediate rooms between the passageway and chamber.<ref name="#1">{{Cite book|language=ja|author=Keiji Nagahara|editor=Eiichi Ishigami|title=Iwanami Japanese History Dictionary|publisher=Iwanami Shoten|year=1999|isbn=4-00-080093-0}}</ref>
In {{ill|Kamakura|ja|鎌倉市}}, Yokohama tombs feature the distinctive "Kamakura-type" (鎌倉型横穴墓), where burial shelves or smaller inner chambers were carved into the rear walls of burial chambers.<ref name="#2">{{Cite book|language=ja|author=Sakae Ward Historical Committee|title=The History of Sakae|publisher=Sakae Ward Community Promotion Division|year=2013}}</ref>
Yokohama tombs are typically found in clusters (横穴墓群, yokohama bokun). The {{ill|Yoshimi Hundred Caves|ja|吉見百穴}} in {{ill|Yoshimi|ja|吉見町}}, {{ill|Saitama Prefecture|ja|埼玉県}}, comprises over 200 tombs and is a prominent example designated as a National Historic Site.
Some tombs also feature wall carvings and paintings, often categorized as decorative kofun. Colored embellishments have been discovered in regions such as [[Kyushu]], [[Kanto]], and parts of [[Tohoku]].
== Origins and Evolution == Yokohama tombs originated in northern Kyushu around the late 5th century during the Kofun period and subsequently spread across western Japan, including the San'in, Sanyo, Kinki, and Tokai regions by the mid-6th century. By the early 7th century, they had reached the Hokuriku, Kanto, and southern Tohoku regions. The practice peaked around the time of the {{ill|Thin Burial Edict|ja|薄葬令}} before declining in the late 8th century.<ref name="#1"/>
== Name == Yokohama tombs are sometimes called "yokoana kofun" (横穴古墳), but technically the term "kofun" refers to Kofuns, which these tombs lack. They are often grouped under broader definitions of kofun but differ significantly in their construction and purpose.<ref name="rekihaku"/>
The term "yokohama tombs" became common in the 1960s, gaining popularity among researchers in eastern Japan, whereas western Japan researchers traditionally referred to them as "yokoana." The term "yokohama" is preferred for consistency.<ref name="rekihaku"/>
== Distribution and Notable Cave Tomb Tombs == These tombs are found from Kyushu through San'in, Kinki, Hokuriku, and Tokai, with a high concentration in [[Southern Kantō]]. The northern limit is thought to be in northern [[Miyagi Prefecture]]. Approximately 3,000 examples exist in [[Shizuoka Prefecture]].

These tombs served as burial chambers in ancient East Asia and are most commonly associated with the [[Kofun period]] in Japan, where this burial type emerged and became widely used.

'''Cave Tombs''' (横穴墓, Yokōbo/Ouketsubo<ref name="rekihaku">{{Cite web|language=ja|url=https://www.rekihaku.city.yokohama.jp/maibun/qa/detail.php?seq=22|title=Q：横穴墓ってなんて読むのですか?|publisher=Yokohama City Foundation for History and Culture|accessdate=2018-07-28}}</ref>) are burial tombs generally carved into slopes or cliffs, typically measuring around 2 meters in height and extending several meters in depth. These tombs served as burial chambers in ancient East Asia and are most commonly associated with the [[Kofun period]] in Japan, where this burial type emerged and became widely used.
== Characteristics == [[File:市ヶ尾横穴墓群B群.JPG|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Ichigao Cave Tomb Cluster|ja|市ヶ尾横穴墓群}} B Cluster: Forecourt and entrance.]] [[File:出山横穴墓群 2009.03.21 - panoramio (5).jpg|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Deyama Graves|ja|出山横穴墓群|ja|出山横穴墓群}}: Interior view of the burial chamber.]] [[File:楊谷寺谷戸横穴墓群11号墓.jpg|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Yōkokuji Valley Cave Tomb Cluster|ja|楊谷寺谷戸横穴墓群}} Tomb 11: House-shaped chamber.]] [[File:長柄横穴群11号墓棺座.JPG|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Nagara Cave Tomb Cluster|ja|長柄横穴群|1=Nagara Cave Tomb Cluster}} Tomb 11: Stone coffin base.]] Yokohama tombs closely resemble [[kofun]] tombs with horizontal stone chambers. They were carved into rock faces, featuring entrances leading to passageways (羨道, sendō), which open into burial chambers (玄室, genshitsu). These tombs typically lack Kofuns but include exceptions. Burial chambers often feature bases for coffins (棺座, kanza) and showcase various ceiling styles, such as house-shaped, dome-shaped, or arch-shaped. Some tombs incorporate forecourts and intermediate rooms between the passageway and chamber.<ref name="#1">{{Cite book|language=ja|author=Keiji Nagahara|editor=Eiichi Ishigami|title=Iwanami Japanese History Dictionary|publisher=Iwanami Shoten|year=1999|isbn=4-00-080093-0}}</ref>
In {{ill|Kamakura|ja|鎌倉市}}, Yokohama tombs feature the distinctive "Kamakura-type" (鎌倉型横穴墓), where burial shelves or smaller inner chambers were carved into the rear walls of burial chambers.<ref name="#2">{{Cite book|language=ja|author=Sakae Ward Historical Committee|title=The History of Sakae|publisher=Sakae Ward Community Promotion Division|year=2013}}</ref>
Yokohama tombs are typically found in clusters (横穴墓群, yokohama bokun). The {{ill|Yoshimi Hundred Caves|ja|吉見百穴}} in {{ill|Yoshimi|ja|吉見町}}, {{ill|Saitama Prefecture|ja|埼玉県}}, comprises over 200 tombs and is a prominent example designated as a National Historic Site.
Some tombs also feature wall carvings and paintings, often categorized as decorative kofun. Colored embellishments have been discovered in regions such as [[Kyushu]], [[Kanto]], and parts of [[Tohoku]].
== Origins and Evolution == Yokohama tombs originated in northern Kyushu around the late 5th century during the Kofun period and subsequently spread across western Japan, including the San'in, Sanyo, Kinki, and Tokai regions by the mid-6th century. By the early 7th century, they had reached the Hokuriku, Kanto, and southern Tohoku regions. The practice peaked around the time of the {{ill|Thin Burial Edict|ja|薄葬令}} before declining in the late 8th century.<ref name="#1"/>
== Name == Yokohama tombs are sometimes called "yokoana kofun" (横穴古墳), but technically the term "kofun" refers to Kofuns, which these tombs lack. They are often grouped under broader definitions of kofun but differ significantly in their construction and purpose.<ref name="rekihaku"/>
The term "yokohama tombs" became common in the 1960s, gaining popularity among researchers in eastern Japan, whereas western Japan researchers traditionally referred to them as "yokoana." The term "yokohama" is preferred for consistency.<ref name="rekihaku"/>
== Distribution and Notable Cave Tomb Tombs == These tombs are found from Kyushu through San'in, Kinki, Hokuriku, and Tokai, with a high concentration in [[Southern Kantō]]. The northern limit is thought to be in northern [[Miyagi Prefecture]]. Approximately 3,000 examples exist in [[Shizuoka Prefecture]].

'''Cave Tombs''' (横穴墓, Yokōbo/Ouketsubo<ref name="rekihaku">{{Cite web|language=ja|url=https://www.rekihaku.city.yokohama.jp/maibun/qa/detail.php?seq=22|title=Q：横穴墓ってなんて読むのですか?|publisher=Yokohama City Foundation for History and Culture|accessdate=2018-07-28}}</ref>) are burial tombs generally carved into slopes or cliffs, typically measuring around 2 meters in height and extending several meters in depth. These tombs served as burial chambers in ancient East Asia and are most commonly associated with the [[Kofun period]] in Japan, where this burial type emerged and became widely used.
== Characteristics == [[File:市ヶ尾横穴墓群B群.JPG|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Ichigao Cave Tomb Cluster|ja|市ヶ尾横穴墓群}} B Cluster: Forecourt and entrance.]] [[File:出山横穴墓群 2009.03.21 - panoramio (5).jpg|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Deyama Graves|ja|出山横穴墓群|ja|出山横穴墓群}}: Interior view of the burial chamber.]] [[File:楊谷寺谷戸横穴墓群11号墓.jpg|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Yōkokuji Valley Cave Tomb Cluster|ja|楊谷寺谷戸横穴墓群}} Tomb 11: House-shaped chamber.]] [[File:長柄横穴群11号墓棺座.JPG|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Nagara Cave Tomb Cluster|ja|長柄横穴群|1=Nagara Cave Tomb Cluster}} Tomb 11: Stone coffin base.]] Yokohama tombs closely resemble [[kofun]] tombs with horizontal stone chambers. They were carved into rock faces, featuring entrances leading to passageways (羨道, sendō), which open into burial chambers (玄室, genshitsu). These tombs typically lack Kofuns but include exceptions. Burial chambers often feature bases for coffins (棺座, kanza) and showcase various ceiling styles, such as house-shaped, dome-shaped, or arch-shaped. Some tombs incorporate forecourts and intermediate rooms between the passageway and chamber.<ref name="#1">{{Cite book|language=ja|author=Keiji Nagahara|editor=Eiichi Ishigami|title=Iwanami Japanese History Dictionary|publisher=Iwanami Shoten|year=1999|isbn=4-00-080093-0}}</ref>
In {{ill|Kamakura|ja|鎌倉市}}, Yokohama tombs feature the distinctive "Kamakura-type" (鎌倉型横穴墓), where burial shelves or smaller inner chambers were carved into the rear walls of burial chambers.<ref name="#2">{{Cite book|language=ja|author=Sakae Ward Historical Committee|title=The History of Sakae|publisher=Sakae Ward Community Promotion Division|year=2013}}</ref>
Yokohama tombs are typically found in clusters (横穴墓群, yokohama bokun). The {{ill|Yoshimi Hundred Caves|ja|吉見百穴}} in {{ill|Yoshimi|ja|吉見町}}, {{ill|Saitama Prefecture|ja|埼玉県}}, comprises over 200 tombs and is a prominent example designated as a National Historic Site.
Some tombs also feature wall carvings and paintings, often categorized as decorative kofun. Colored embellishments have been discovered in regions such as [[Kyushu]], [[Kanto]], and parts of [[Tohoku]].
== Origins and Evolution == Yokohama tombs originated in northern Kyushu around the late 5th century during the Kofun period and subsequently spread across western Japan, including the San'in, Sanyo, Kinki, and Tokai regions by the mid-6th century. By the early 7th century, they had reached the Hokuriku, Kanto, and southern Tohoku regions. The practice peaked around the time of the {{ill|Thin Burial Edict|ja|薄葬令}} before declining in the late 8th century.<ref name="#1"/>
== Name == Yokohama tombs are sometimes called "yokoana kofun" (横穴古墳), but technically the term "kofun" refers to Kofuns, which these tombs lack. They are often grouped under broader definitions of kofun but differ significantly in their construction and purpose.<ref name="rekihaku"/>
The term "yokohama tombs" became common in the 1960s, gaining popularity among researchers in eastern Japan, whereas western Japan researchers traditionally referred to them as "yokoana." The term "yokohama" is preferred for consistency.<ref name="rekihaku"/>
== Distribution and Notable Cave Tomb Tombs == These tombs are found from Kyushu through San'in, Kinki, Hokuriku, and Tokai, with a high concentration in [[Southern Kantō]]. The northern limit is thought to be in northern [[Miyagi Prefecture]]. Approximately 3,000 examples exist in [[Shizuoka Prefecture]].

'''Cave Tombs''' (横穴墓, Yokōbo/Ouketsubo<ref name="rekihaku">{{Cite web|language=ja|url=https://www.rekihaku.city.yokohama.jp/maibun/qa/detail.php?seq=22|title=Q：横穴墓ってなんて読むのですか?|publisher=Yokohama City Foundation for History and Culture|accessdate=2018-07-28}}</ref>) are burial tombs generally carved into slopes or cliffs, typically measuring around 2 meters in height and extending several meters in depth. These tombs served as burial chambers in ancient East Asia and are most commonly associated with the [[Kofun period]] in Japan, where this burial type emerged and became widely used.
== Characteristics == [[File:市ヶ尾横穴墓群B群.JPG|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Ichigao Cave Tomb Cluster|ja|市ヶ尾横穴墓群}} B Cluster: Forecourt and entrance.]] [[File:出山横穴墓群 2009.03.21 - panoramio (5).jpg|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Deyama Graves|ja|出山横穴墓群|ja|出山横穴墓群}}: Interior view of the burial chamber.]] [[File:楊谷寺谷戸横穴墓群11号墓.jpg|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Yōkokuji Valley Cave Tomb Cluster|ja|楊谷寺谷戸横穴墓群}} Tomb 11: House-shaped chamber.]] [[File:長柄横穴群11号墓棺座.JPG|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Nagara Cave Tomb Cluster|ja|長柄横穴群|1=Nagara Cave Tomb Cluster}} Tomb 11: Stone coffin base.]] Yokohama tombs closely resemble [[kofun]] tombs with horizontal stone chambers. They were carved into rock faces, featuring entrances leading to passageways (羨道, sendō), which open into burial chambers (玄室, genshitsu). These tombs typically lack Kofuns but include exceptions. Burial chambers often feature bases for coffins (棺座, kanza) and showcase various ceiling styles, such as house-shaped, dome-shaped, or arch-shaped. Some tombs incorporate forecourts and intermediate rooms between the passageway and chamber.<ref name="#1">{{Cite book|language=ja|author=Keiji Nagahara|editor=Eiichi Ishigami|title=Iwanami Japanese History Dictionary|publisher=Iwanami Shoten|year=1999|isbn=4-00-080093-0}}</ref>
In {{ill|Kamakura|ja|鎌倉市}}, Yokohama tombs feature the distinctive "Kamakura-type" (鎌倉型横穴墓), where burial shelves or smaller inner chambers were carved into the rear walls of burial chambers.<ref name="#2">{{Cite book|language=ja|author=Sakae Ward Historical Committee|title=The History of Sakae|publisher=Sakae Ward Community Promotion Division|year=2013}}</ref>
Yokohama tombs are typically found in clusters (横穴墓群, yokohama bokun). The {{ill|Yoshimi Hundred Caves|ja|吉見百穴}} in {{ill|Yoshimi|ja|吉見町}}, {{ill|Saitama Prefecture|ja|埼玉県}}, comprises over 200 tombs and is a prominent example designated as a National Historic Site.
Some tombs also feature wall carvings and paintings, often categorized as decorative kofun. Colored embellishments have been discovered in regions such as [[Kyushu]], [[Kanto]], and parts of [[Tohoku]].
== Origins and Evolution == Yokohama tombs originated in northern Kyushu around the late 5th century during the Kofun period and subsequently spread across western Japan, including the San'in, Sanyo, Kinki, and Tokai regions by the mid-6th century. By the early 7th century, they had reached the Hokuriku, Kanto, and southern Tohoku regions. The practice peaked around the time of the {{ill|Thin Burial Edict|ja|薄葬令}} before declining in the late 8th century.<ref name="#1"/>
== Name == Yokohama tombs are sometimes called "yokoana kofun" (横穴古墳), but technically the term "kofun" refers to Kofuns, which these tombs lack. They are often grouped under broader definitions of kofun but differ significantly in their construction and purpose.<ref name="rekihaku"/>
The term "yokohama tombs" became common in the 1960s, gaining popularity among researchers in eastern Japan, whereas western Japan researchers traditionally referred to them as "yokoana." The term "yokohama" is preferred for consistency.<ref name="rekihaku"/>
== Distribution and Notable Cave Tomb Tombs == These tombs are found from Kyushu through San'in, Kinki, Hokuriku, and Tokai, with a high concentration in [[Southern Kantō]]. The northern limit is thought to be in northern [[Miyagi Prefecture]]. Approximately 3,000 examples exist in [[Shizuoka Prefecture]].

Here is the text I pasted on numerous Kofun related articles {{nihongo|{{ill|Corridor-type kofun|lt=Corridor-type kofun|ja|横穴墓|12=draft}}|横穴式石室|yokoana-shiki sekishitsu}}. I find it rather absurd that I did that as it is relatively blatantly wrong, but I did not properly check. I am making a disambiguation page at [[Corridor-type kofun]] that should be imported into wikipedia too, and we should sort out this issue before publishing either article for fear of having [[User:Cewbot]] correct the template to the wrong thing. Maybe just a mass replace of that text to [[Corridor-type kofun]] linking to the disambiguation page so disambiguation page fixer people can determine which one it is going to.[[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 04:24, 30 March 2025 (UTC)}} {{afc comment|1=Contrast with {{ill|Yokoana-shiki sekishitsu|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|12=draft}} on enwiki I accidentally conflated Cave tombs and {{ill|Yokoana-shiki sekishitsu|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|12=draft}}s a lot but these are distinct[[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 03:15, 27 February 2025 (UTC)}} {{afc comment|1=The category [[:Category:Corridor-type kofun]] was one that I made on enwiki with the erroneous association with {{ill|Yokoana-shiki sekishitsu|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|12=draft}}s. If this is ever approved as an enwiki article, immediately run a speedy renaming on that category. Likewise check all links already on enwiki because they are ambiguous between the two articles, apparently even in terms of having both kanji in them, idk how I did something so dumb back then[[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 01:42, 15 March 2025 (UTC)}} [[File:Yoshimi Yoshimi-hyakuana 2.JPG|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Yoshimi Hundred Caves|ja|吉見百穴|12=draft}} (November 2010)]] [[File:柏谷横穴群.JPG|right|250px|thumb|{{ill|Kashiya Cave Tombs|ja|柏谷横穴群|12=draft}} (February 2013)]] '''Cave Tombs''' (横穴墓, Yokōbo/Ouketsubo<ref name="rekihaku">{{Cite web|language=ja|url=https://www.rekihaku.city.yokohama.jp/maibun/qa/detail.php?seq=22|title=Q：横穴墓ってなんて読むのですか?|publisher=Yokohama City Foundation for History and Culture|accessdate=2018-07-28}}</ref>) are burial tombs generally carved into slopes or cliffs, typically measuring around 2 meters in height and extending several meters in depth. These tombs served as burial chambers in ancient East Asia and are most commonly associated with the [[Kofun period]] in Japan, where this burial type emerged and became widely used. == Characteristics == [[File:市ヶ尾横穴墓群B群.JPG|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Ichigao Cave Tomb Cluster|ja|市ヶ尾横穴墓群|12=draft}} B Cluster: Forecourt and entrance.]] [[File:出山横穴墓群 2009.03.21 - panoramio (5).jpg|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Deyama Graves|ja|出山横穴墓群|ja|出山横穴墓群|12=draft}}: Interior view of the burial chamber.]] [[File:楊谷寺谷戸横穴墓群11号墓.jpg|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Yōkokuji Valley Cave Tomb Cluster|ja|楊谷寺谷戸横穴墓群|12=draft}} Tomb 11: House-shaped chamber.]] [[File:長柄横穴群11号墓棺座.JPG|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Nagara Cave Tomb Cluster|ja|長柄横穴群|1=Nagara Cave Tomb Cluster|12=draft}} Tomb 11: Stone coffin base.]] Yokohama tombs closely resemble [[kofun]] tombs with horizontal stone chambers. They were carved into rock faces, featuring entrances leading to passageways (羨道, sendō), which open into burial chambers (玄室, genshitsu). These tombs typically lack Kofuns but include exceptions. Burial chambers often feature bases for coffins (棺座, kanza) and showcase various ceiling styles, such as house-shaped, dome-shaped, or arch-shaped. Some tombs incorporate forecourts and intermediate rooms between the passageway and chamber.<ref name="#1">{{Cite book|language=ja|author=Keiji Nagahara|editor=Eiichi Ishigami|title=Iwanami Japanese History Dictionary|publisher=Iwanami Shoten|year=1999|isbn=4-00-080093-0}}</ref> In {{ill|Kamakura|ja|鎌倉市|12=draft}}, Yokohama tombs feature the distinctive "Kamakura-type" (鎌倉型横穴墓), where burial shelves or smaller inner chambers were carved into the rear walls of burial chambers.<ref name="#2">{{Cite book|language=ja|author=Sakae Ward Historical Committee|title=The History of Sakae|publisher=Sakae Ward Community Promotion Division|year=2013}}</ref> Yokohama tombs are typically found in clusters (横穴墓群, yokohama bokun). The {{ill|Yoshimi Hundred Caves|ja|吉見百穴|12=draft}} in {{ill|Yoshimi|ja|吉見町|12=draft}}, {{ill|Saitama Prefecture|ja|埼玉県|12=draft}}, comprises over 200 tombs and is a prominent example designated as a National Historic Site. Some tombs also feature wall carvings and paintings, often categorized as decorative kofun. Colored embellishments have been discovered in regions such as [[Kyushu]], [[Kanto]], and parts of [[Tohoku]]. == Origins and Evolution == Yokohama tombs originated in northern Kyushu around the late 5th century during the Kofun period and subsequently spread across western Japan, including the San'in, Sanyo, Kinki, and Tokai regions by the mid-6th century. By the early 7th century, they had reached the Hokuriku, Kanto, and southern Tohoku regions. The practice peaked around the time of the {{ill|Thin Burial Edict|ja|薄葬令|12=draft}} before declining in the late 8th century.<ref name="#1"/> == Name == Yokohama tombs are sometimes called "yokoana kofun" (横穴古墳), but technically the term "kofun" refers to Kofuns, which these tombs lack. They are often grouped under broader definitions of kofun but differ significantly in their construction and purpose.<ref name="rekihaku"/> The term "yokohama tombs" became common in the 1960s, gaining popularity among researchers in eastern Japan, whereas western Japan researchers traditionally referred to them as "yokoana." The term "yokohama" is preferred for consistency.<ref name="rekihaku"/> == Distribution and Notable Cave Tomb Tombs == These tombs are found from Kyushu through San'in, Kinki, Hokuriku, and Tokai, with a high concentration in [[Southern Kantō]]. The northern limit is thought to be in northern [[Miyagi Prefecture]]. Approximately 3,000 examples exist in [[Shizuoka Prefecture]]. === Tōhoku Region === * {{ill|Yamahata Cave Tomb Cluster|ja|山畑横穴群|12=draft}} ({{ill|Ōsaki, Miyagi|ja|大崎市|12=draft}}, [[Miyagi Prefecture]]) - Likewise check all links already on enwiki because they are ambiguous between the two articles, apparently even in terms of having both kanji in them, idk how I did something so dumb back then[[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 01:42, 15 March 2025 (UTC)}} [[File:Yoshimi Yoshimi-hyakuana 2.JPG|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Yoshimi Hundred Caves|ja|吉見百穴|12=draft}} (November 2010)]] [[File:柏谷横穴群.JPG|right|250px|thumb|{{ill|Kashiya Cave Tombs|ja|柏谷横穴群|12=draft}} (February 2013)]] '''Cave Tombs''' (横穴墓, Yokōbo/Ouketsubo<ref name="rekihaku">{{Cite web|language=ja|url=https://www.rekihaku.city.yokohama.jp/maibun/qa/detail.php?seq=22|title=Q：横穴墓ってなんて読むのですか?|publisher=Yokohama City Foundation for History and Culture|accessdate=2018-07-28}}</ref>) are burial tombs generally carved into slopes or cliffs, typically measuring around 2 meters in height and extending several meters in depth. These tombs served as burial chambers in ancient East Asia and are most commonly associated with the [[Kofun period]] in Japan, where this burial type emerged and became widely used. == Characteristics == [[File:市ヶ尾横穴墓群B群.JPG|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Ichigao Cave Tomb Cluster|ja|市ヶ尾横穴墓群|12=draft}} B Cluster: Forecourt and entrance.]] [[File:出山横穴墓群 2009.03.21 - panoramio (5).jpg|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Deyama Graves|ja|出山横穴墓群|ja|出山横穴墓群|12=draft}}: Interior view of the burial chamber.]] [[File:楊谷寺谷戸横穴墓群11号墓.jpg|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Yōkokuji Valley Cave Tomb Cluster|ja|楊谷寺谷戸横穴墓群|12=draft}} Tomb 11: House-shaped chamber.]] [[File:長柄横穴群11号墓棺座.JPG|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Nagara Cave Tomb Cluster|ja|長柄横穴群|1=Nagara Cave Tomb Cluster|12=draft}} Tomb 11: Stone coffin base.]] Yokohama tombs closely resemble [[kofun]] tombs with horizontal stone chambers. They were carved into rock faces, featuring entrances leading to passageways (羨道, sendō), which open into burial chambers (玄室, genshitsu). These tombs typically lack Kofuns but include exceptions. Burial chambers often feature bases for coffins (棺座, kanza) and showcase various ceiling styles, such as house-shaped, dome-shaped, or arch-shaped. Some tombs incorporate forecourts and intermediate rooms between the passageway and chamber.<ref name="#1">{{Cite book|language=ja|author=Keiji Nagahara|editor=Eiichi Ishigami|title=Iwanami Japanese History Dictionary|publisher=Iwanami Shoten|year=1999|isbn=4-00-080093-0}}</ref> In {{ill|Kamakura|ja|鎌倉市|12=draft}}, Yokohama tombs feature the distinctive "Kamakura-type" (鎌倉型横穴墓), where burial shelves or smaller inner chambers were carved into the rear walls of burial chambers.<ref name="#2">{{Cite book|language=ja|author=Sakae Ward Historical Committee|title=The History of Sakae|publisher=Sakae Ward Community Promotion Division|year=2013}}</ref> Yokohama tombs are typically found in clusters (横穴墓群, yokohama bokun). The {{ill|Yoshimi Hundred Caves|ja|吉見百穴|12=draft}} in {{ill|Yoshimi|ja|吉見町|12=draft}}, {{ill|Saitama Prefecture|ja|埼玉県|12=draft}}, comprises over 200 tombs and is a prominent example designated as a National Historic Site. Some tombs also feature wall carvings and paintings, often categorized as decorative kofun. Colored embellishments have been discovered in regions such as [[Kyushu]], [[Kanto]], and parts of [[Tohoku]]. == Origins and Evolution == Yokohama tombs originated in northern Kyushu around the late 5th century during the Kofun period and subsequently spread across western Japan, including the San'in, Sanyo, Kinki, and Tokai regions by the mid-6th century. By the early 7th century, they had reached the Hokuriku, Kanto, and southern Tohoku regions. The practice peaked around the time of the {{ill|Thin Burial Edict|ja|薄葬令|12=draft}} before declining in the late 8th century.<ref name="#1"/> == Name == Yokohama tombs are sometimes called "yokoana kofun" (横穴古墳), but technically the term "kofun" refers to Kofuns, which these tombs lack. They are often grouped under broader definitions of kofun but differ significantly in their construction and purpose.<ref name="rekihaku"/> The term "yokohama tombs" became common in the 1960s, gaining popularity among researchers in eastern Japan, whereas western Japan researchers traditionally referred to them as "yokoana." The term "yokohama" is preferred for consistency.<ref name="rekihaku"/> == Distribution and Notable Cave Tomb Tombs == These tombs are found from Kyushu through San'in, Kinki, Hokuriku, and Tokai, with a high concentration in [[Southern Kantō]]. The northern limit is thought to be in northern [[Miyagi Prefecture]]. {{distinguish|{{ill|Yokoana-shiki sekishitsu|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|12=draft}}}} {{afc comment|1=To be clear for both of these articles. Here is the text I pasted on numerous Kofun related articles {{nihongo|{{ill|Corridor-type kofun|lt=Corridor-type kofun|ja|横穴墓|12=draft}}|横穴式石室|yokoana-shiki sekishitsu}}. I find it rather absurd that I did that as it is relatively blatantly wrong, but I did not properly check. I am making a disambiguation page at [[Corridor-type kofun]] that should be imported into wikipedia too, and we should sort out this issue before publishing either article for fear of having [[User:Cewbot]] correct the template to the wrong thing. Maybe just a mass replace of that text to [[Corridor-type kofun]] linking to the disambiguation page so disambiguation page fixer people can determine which one it is going to.[[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 04:24, 30 March 2025 (UTC)}} {{afc comment|1=Contrast with {{ill|Yokoana-shiki sekishitsu|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|12=draft}} on enwiki I accidentally conflated Cave tombs and {{ill|Yokoana-shiki sekishitsu|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|12=draft}}s a lot but these are distinct[[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 03:15, 27 February 2025 (UTC)}} {{afc comment|1=The category [[:Category:Corridor-type kofun]] was one that I made on enwiki with the erroneous association with {{ill|Yokoana-shiki sekishitsu|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|12=draft}}s. If this is ever approved as an enwiki article, immediately run a speedy renaming on that category. Likewise check all links already on enwiki because they are ambiguous between the two articles, apparently even in terms of having both kanji in them, idk how I did something so dumb back then[[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 01:42, 15 March 2025 (UTC)}} [[File:Yoshimi Yoshimi-hyakuana 2.JPG|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Yoshimi Hundred Caves|ja|吉見百穴|12=draft}} (November 2010)]] [[File:柏谷横穴群.JPG|right|250px|thumb|{{ill|Kashiya Cave Tombs|ja|柏谷横穴群|12=draft}} (February 2013)]] '''Cave Tombs''' (横穴墓, Yokōbo/Ouketsubo<ref name="rekihaku">{{Cite web|language=ja|url=https://www.rekihaku.city.yokohama.jp/maibun/qa/detail.php?seq=22|title=Q：横穴墓ってなんて読むのですか?|publisher=Yokohama City Foundation for History and Culture|accessdate=2018-07-28}}</ref>) are burial tombs generally carved into slopes or cliffs, typically measuring around 2 meters in height and extending several meters in depth. These tombs served as burial chambers in ancient East Asia and are most commonly associated with the [[Kofun period]] in Japan, where this burial type emerged and became widely used. == Characteristics == [[File:市ヶ尾横穴墓群B群.JPG|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Ichigao Cave Tomb Cluster|ja|市ヶ尾横穴墓群|12=draft}} B Cluster: Forecourt and entrance.]] [[File:出山横穴墓群 2009.03.21 - panoramio (5).jpg|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Deyama Graves|ja|出山横穴墓群|ja|出山横穴墓群|12=draft}}: Interior view of the burial chamber.]] [[File:楊谷寺谷戸横穴墓群11号墓.jpg|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Yōkokuji Valley Cave Tomb Cluster|ja|楊谷寺谷戸横穴墓群|12=draft}} Tomb 11: House-shaped chamber.]] [[File:長柄横穴群11号墓棺座.JPG|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Nagara Cave Tomb Cluster|ja|長柄横穴群|1=Nagara Cave Tomb Cluster|12=draft}} Tomb 11: Stone coffin base.]] Yokohama tombs closely resemble [[kofun]] tombs with horizontal stone chambers. They were carved into rock faces, featuring entrances leading to passageways (羨道, sendō), which open into burial chambers (玄室, genshitsu). These tombs typically lack Kofuns but include exceptions. Burial chambers often feature bases for coffins (棺座, kanza) and showcase various ceiling styles, such as house-shaped, dome-shaped, or arch-shaped. Some tombs incorporate forecourts and intermediate rooms between the passageway and chamber.<ref name="#1">{{Cite book|language=ja|author=Keiji Nagahara|editor=Eiichi Ishigami|title=Iwanami Japanese History Dictionary|publisher=Iwanami Shoten|year=1999|isbn=4-00-080093-0}}</ref> In {{ill|Kamakura|ja|鎌倉市|12=draft}}, Yokohama tombs feature the distinctive "Kamakura-type" (鎌倉型横穴墓), where burial shelves or smaller inner chambers were carved into the rear walls of burial chambers.<ref name="#2">{{Cite book|language=ja|author=Sakae Ward Historical Committee|title=The History of Sakae|publisher=Sakae Ward Community Promotion Division|year=2013}}</ref> Yokohama tombs are typically found in clusters (横穴墓群, yokohama bokun). The {{ill|Yoshimi Hundred Caves|ja|吉見百穴|12=draft}} in {{ill|Yoshimi|ja|吉見町|12=draft}}, {{ill|Saitama Prefecture|ja|埼玉県|12=draft}}, comprises over 200 tombs and is a prominent example designated as a National Historic Site. Some tombs also feature wall carvings and paintings, often categorized as decorative kofun. Colored embellishments have been discovered in regions such as [[Kyushu]], [[Kanto]], and parts of [[Tohoku]]. == Origins and Evolution == Yokohama tombs originated in northern Kyushu around the late 5th century during the Kofun period and subsequently spread across western Japan, including the San'in, Sanyo, Kinki, and Tokai regions by the mid-6th century. By the early 7th century, they had reached the Hokuriku, Kanto, and southern Tohoku regions. The practice peaked around the time of the {{ill|Thin Burial Edict|ja|薄葬令|12=draft}} before declining in the late 8th century.<ref name="#1"/> == Name == Yokohama tombs are sometimes called "yokoana kofun" (横穴古墳), but technically the term "kofun" refers to Kofuns, which these tombs lack. They are often grouped under broader definitions of kofun but differ significantly in their construction and purpose.<ref name="rekihaku"/> The term "yokohama tombs" became common in the 1960s, gaining popularity among researchers in eastern Japan, whereas western Japan researchers traditionally referred to them as "yokoana." The term "yokohama" is preferred for consistency.<ref name="rekihaku"/> == Distribution and Notable Cave Tomb Tombs == These tombs are found from Kyushu through San'in, Kinki, Hokuriku, and Tokai, with a high concentration in [[Southern Kantō]]. The northern limit is thought to be in northern [[Miyagi Prefecture]]. Approximately 3,000 examples exist in [[Shizuoka Prefecture]]. === Tōhoku Region === * {{ill|Yamahata Cave Tomb Cluster|ja|山畑横穴群|12=draft}} ({{ill|Ōsaki, Miyagi|ja|大崎市|12=draft}}, [[Miyagi Prefecture]]) - National Historic Site, 26 tombs * {{ill|Atagoyama Cave Tombs|ja|愛宕山横穴墓群|ja|愛宕山横穴墓群|12=draft}} ({{ill|Taihaku-ku, Sendai|ja|太白区|12=draft}}, {{ill|Sendai|ja|仙台市|12=draft}}) * {{ill|Mogasaki Cave Tomb Cluster|ja|茂ヶ崎横穴墓群|12=draft}} (Taihaku-ku, Sendai) - If this is ever approved as an enwiki article, immediately run a speedy renaming on that category. Likewise check all links already on enwiki because they are ambiguous between the two articles, apparently even in terms of having both kanji in them, idk how I did something so dumb back then[[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 01:42, 15 March 2025 (UTC)|qq=}} [[File:Yoshimi Yoshimi-hyakuana 2.JPG|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Yoshimi Hundred Caves|ja|吉見百穴|qq=|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} (November 2010)]] [[File:柏谷横穴群.JPG|right|250px|thumb|{{ill|Kashiya Cave Tombs|ja|柏谷横穴群|qq=|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} (February 2013)]] '''Cave Tombs''' (横穴墓, Yokōbo/Ouketsubo<ref name="rekihaku">{{Cite web|language=ja|url=https://www.rekihaku.city.yokohama.jp/maibun/qa/detail.php?seq=22|title=Q：横穴墓ってなんて読むのですか?|publisher=Yokohama City Foundation for History and Culture|accessdate=2018-07-28|qq=}}</ref>) are burial tombs generally carved into slopes or cliffs, typically measuring around 2 meters in height and extending several meters in depth. These tombs served as burial chambers in ancient East Asia and are most commonly associated with the [[Kofun period]] in Japan, where this burial type emerged and became widely used. == Characteristics == [[File:市ヶ尾横穴墓群B群.JPG|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Ichigao Cave Tomb Cluster|ja|市ヶ尾横穴墓群|qq=|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} B Cluster: Forecourt and entrance.]] [[File:出山横穴墓群 2009.03.21 - panoramio (5).jpg|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Deyama Graves|ja|出山横穴墓群|ja|出山横穴墓群|qq=|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}: Interior view of the burial chamber.]] [[File:楊谷寺谷戸横穴墓群11号墓.jpg|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Yōkokuji Valley Cave Tomb Cluster|ja|楊谷寺谷戸横穴墓群|qq=|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} Tomb 11: House-shaped chamber.]] [[File:長柄横穴群11号墓棺座.JPG|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Nagara Cave Tomb Cluster|ja|長柄横穴群|1=Nagara Cave Tomb Cluster|qq=|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} Tomb 11: Stone coffin base.]] Yokohama tombs closely resemble [[kofun]] tombs with horizontal stone chambers. They were carved into rock faces, featuring entrances leading to passageways (羨道, sendō), which open into burial chambers (玄室, genshitsu). These tombs typically lack Kofuns but include exceptions. Burial chambers often feature bases for coffins (棺座, kanza) and showcase various ceiling styles, such as house-shaped, dome-shaped, or arch-shaped. Some tombs incorporate forecourts and intermediate rooms between the passageway and chamber.<ref name="#1">{{Cite book|language=ja|author=Keiji Nagahara|editor=Eiichi Ishigami|title=Iwanami Japanese History Dictionary|publisher=Iwanami Shoten|year=1999|isbn=4-00-080093-0|qq=}}</ref> In {{ill|Kamakura|ja|鎌倉市|qq=|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}, Yokohama tombs feature the distinctive "Kamakura-type" (鎌倉型横穴墓), where burial shelves or smaller inner chambers were carved into the rear walls of burial chambers.<ref name="#2">{{Cite book|language=ja|author=Sakae Ward Historical Committee|title=The History of Sakae|publisher=Sakae Ward Community Promotion Division|year=2013|qq=}}</ref> Yokohama tombs are typically found in clusters (横穴墓群, yokohama bokun). The {{ill|Yoshimi Hundred Caves|ja|吉見百穴|qq=|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} in {{ill|Yoshimi|ja|吉見町|qq=|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|Saitama Prefecture|ja|埼玉県|qq=|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}, comprises over 200 tombs and is a prominent example designated as a National Historic Site. Some tombs also feature wall carvings and paintings, often categorized as decorative kofun. Colored embellishments have been discovered in regions such as [[Kyushu]], [[Kanto]], and parts of [[Tohoku]]. == Origins and Evolution == Yokohama tombs originated in northern Kyushu around the late 5th century during the Kofun period and subsequently spread across western Japan, including the San'in, Sanyo, Kinki, and Tokai regions by the mid-6th century. By the early 7th century, they had reached the Hokuriku, Kanto, and southern Tohoku regions. The practice peaked around the time of the {{ill|Thin Burial Edict|ja|薄葬令|qq=|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} before declining in the late 8th century.<ref name="#1"/> == Name == Yokohama tombs are sometimes called "yokoana kofun" (横穴古墳), but technically the term "kofun" refers to Kofuns, which these tombs lack. They are often grouped under broader definitions of kofun but differ significantly in their construction and purpose.<ref name="rekihaku"/> The term "yokohama tombs" became common in the 1960s, gaining popularity among researchers in eastern Japan, whereas western Japan researchers traditionally referred to them as "yokoana." The term "yokohama" is preferred for consistency.<ref name="rekihaku"/> == Distribution and Notable Cave Tomb Tombs == These tombs are found from Kyushu through San'in, Kinki, Hokuriku, and Tokai, with a high concentration in [[Southern Kantō]]. The northern limit is thought to be in northern [[Miyagi Prefecture]].
